title: R Post
text:
1. Data Cleaning and Preparation
We load the palmerpenguins package alongside tidyverse to filter out missing records and inspect key variables.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

# Clean dataset removing NA values in body metrics
penguins_clean <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(species, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, sex) %>%
  mutate(
    species = as.character(species),
    bill_ratio = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm
  )

glimpse(penguins_clean)

title: About
text: I grew up with a background in engineering and geographic information science, completing my Bachelor of Engineering in Surveying and Mapping Engineering at Tongji University followed by a Master of Science in GIS at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Before starting the Master of Data Science (MDS) program at UBC, I worked as a GIS Developer at Mississippi State University’s Geosystems Research Institute. My work focused on full-stack geospatial application development, spatial statistics, and database architecture—building interactive decision-support tools like the Conservation Reserve Program Menu Tool and regional spatial analytics platforms.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science
Throughout my work with spatial systems, I found that the most compelling challenges always came down to data: extracting signal from massive spatial datasets, building robust statistical models, and automating complex analytical pipelines. While GIS gave me a strong foundation in spatial analysis and visualization, I joined the MDS program at UBC to formalize and expand my toolkit in machine learning, high-performance computing, and structured data engineering. My goal is to bridge complex data science methodologies with real-world spatial and environmental problem-solving.

title: About

Outside of Data Science
Outside of coursework and coding, I enjoy photography, exploring local food spots, and traveling—with recent trips taking me through New Zealand, Japan, and California. On weekends, you’ll usually find me trying out new restaurants around Richmond and Vancouver, editing photos, or catching up on road trips and outdoor exploring.

title: Combining R and Python with Reticulate
text:
Data science teams frequently use both R and Python for their unique strengths—such as ggplot2 for high-quality visualizations in R and scikit-learn for machine learning in Python.
In this post, we demonstrate how to bridge both execution engines seamlessly within a single Quarto document using the reticulate package.
The dataset used is the palmerpenguins dataset, collected by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station LTER. You can read more on the official palmerpenguins documentation page.

In this post, we demonstrate how to bridge both execution engines seamlessly within a single Quarto document using the reticulate package.

title: Combining R and Python with Reticulate
text:
1. Data Preparation in R
We start in an R chunk by loading palmerpenguins, cleaning missing records, and computing species-level baseline aggregates.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(reticulate)

# Clean dataset removing NAs across key physical measurements
penguins_clean <- penguins %>%
  drop_na(species, bill_length_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) %>%
  mutate(species = as.character(species))

# Calculate summary metrics by species in R
species_summary <- penguins_clean %>%
  group_by(species) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_flipper_mm = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    mean_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    mean_bill_len_mm = mean(bill_length_mm),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

section: 2. Model Fitting in Python (Reading R Objects)
text:
2. Model Fitting in Python (Reading R Objects)
Python accesses that R summary object directly using r.species_summary, fits a linear regression model on raw penguin data passed from R, and computes predicted values.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

# Access R summary object in Python
print("Accessing R species_summary inside Python:")

Accessing R species_summary inside Python:

print(r.species_summary)

1  Chinstrap   68       195.823529  3733.088235         48.833824
2     Gentoo  123       217.186992  5076.016260         47.504878

# Convert R dataframe to Python DataFrame
df_py = r.penguins_clean

# Define predictor features (X) and target variable (y)
X = df_py[['flipper_length_mm', 'bill_length_mm']]
y = df_py['body_mass_g']

# Fit Linear Regression model in Python
model = LinearRegression()
model.fit(X, y)

title: Combining R and Python with Reticulate
section: 3. Visualizing Python Predictions Back in R
text:
3. Visualizing Python Predictions Back in R
R retrieves the Python model results via py$predictions and renders the final comparative plot using ggplot2.

library(ggplot2)

# Access Python object in R using py$...
penguin_preds <- py$df_py

ggplot(penguin_preds, aes(x = body_mass_g, y = predicted_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", size = 0.8) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted Body Mass Across Penguin Species",
    subtitle = "Model fit in Python (scikit-learn) and plotted in R (ggplot2)",
    x = "Actual Body Mass (g)",
    y = "Predicted Body Mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

1. Data Loading & Cleaning
First, load the dataset using palmerpenguins and clean it by removing rows with missing physical measurements.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from palmerpenguins import load_penguins

# Load raw penguins dataset
df_raw = load_penguins()

# Clean missing values across key physical traits
features = ['species', 'island', 'bill_length_mm', 'bill_depth_mm', 'flipper_length_mm', 'body_mass_g', 'sex']
penguins = df_raw.dropna(subset=features).copy()

Figure 1: Flipper Length vs. Body Mass across Palmer Penguin Species.





Summary of Results Strong Linear Relationship: There is a clear positive correlation between flipper length and body mass across all species.
Cluster Separation: Gentoo penguins form a distinct cluster in the upper-right corner (longer flippers, larger body mass), whereas Adelie and Chinstrap penguins overlap considerably in body mass but show separation along bill length and flipper length dimensions.
Sexual Dimorphism: Within every species, male penguins systematically exhibit higher body mass and longer flipper lengths than females.
